sentences.t: Swā se ðēodkyning þēawum lyfde;
sentences.l: So the people-king lived by customs;
sentences.i: So the king of the people lived by good custom;
sentences.n: This line sums up what Beowulf says of Hrothgar’s conduct in his report to Higelāc, which began at 2000 and runs to 2151; the lines after it say what Hrothgar gave him. Hrothgar is the ‘ðēodkyning’, ‘people-king’ (‘ðēod’ ‘people’ + ‘cyning’ ‘king’). ‘þēawum’ is a dative plural, ‘by customs’, with ‘lyfde’, the past of ‘lifian’, ‘live’. ‘þēaw’ is ‘custom, habit, manner of conduct’ and often means good conduct in particular, so the line says that Hrothgar behaved as a king should; that is my reading of the sense, not something the word forces.

sentences.l: not at all had I lost those rewards, the reward of strength, but he gave me treasures, the son of Healfdene, to my own choosing;
sentences.i: I did not at all go without those rewards, the pay for my strength; no, the son of Healfdene gave me treasures to choose as I judged best;
sentences.n: ‘nealles’ is ‘not at all’; ‘forloren hæfde’ is a pluperfect, ‘had lost’, from ‘forlēosan’, with the dative ‘ðām lēanum’, ‘those rewards’. ‘mægnes mēde’, ‘reward of strength’ (genitive ‘mægnes’, ‘mēde’ a feminine dative singular), stands loosely beside ‘lēanum’ as a second name for the same thing, though one is plural and one singular. ‘ac’ is ‘but’, and ‘sunu Healfdenes’ is Hrothgar again, in apposition to ‘hē’. Klaeber restores letters lost in the burned edge: ‘(māðma)s’, Kemble’s supplement, and ‘(mīn)ne’, where Grundtvig reads ‘(sīn)ne’, ‘his own’, instead of ‘my own’. ‘on mīnne sylfes dōm’ is ‘to my own self’s judgement’, that is, ‘dōm’ as ‘decision, discretion’: Hrothgar left the choice to Beowulf. The same word means ‘glory’ at 2179, and that this is the sense of the idiom here is a reading I take from the context.

sentences.t:
ðā ic ðē, beorncyning, bringan wylle,
ēstum geȳwan.
sentences.l: those I to you, warrior-king, will bring, graciously present.
sentences.i: These I mean to bring to you, warrior-king, and to present with a willing heart.
sentences.n: ‘ðā’ is ‘those’, the accusative plural (the form is the same in every gender), picking up the treasures of 2146, not ‘then’; it is the object of ‘bringan’ and ‘geȳwan’, two infinitives after ‘wylle’, ‘am willing to, will’. ‘beorncyning’ is a vocative, ‘warrior-king’ (‘beorn’ ‘warrior, man’), Higelāc. ‘ēstum’ is a dative plural, ‘with favours’, so ‘graciously’; the same word is the ‘ēst’ of 2157 and 2165. ‘geȳwan’ is ‘show, display’, here ‘present’. The stop after ‘geȳwan’ is Klaeber’s full stop, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
Gēn is eall æt ðē
[mīnra] lissa gelong;
sentences.l: Still is all with you of my favours dependent;
sentences.i: All my happiness still rests with you;
sentences.n: ‘Gēn’ is ‘still, yet’. ‘eall’ is the subject and ‘gelong’ a predicate adjective, ‘dependent on, belonging to’ (cf. ‘along’), with ‘æt ðē’, ‘at you’, so ‘with you’. ‘lissa’ is a genitive plural of ‘liss’, ‘kindness, favour, joy’, and Klaeber puts ‘mīnra’, ‘my’, in square brackets: that word is not in the manuscript, and Holthausen (with Chambers) added it; Sievers would instead print ‘gelong[ra]’, and Holthausen at another time read ‘gelenge’ for ‘gelong’ (apparatus). Either way the sense is that what pleases Beowulf depends on Higelāc. ‘lissa’ as ‘favours, joys’ is a guess between two senses of ‘liss’.

sentences.t:
ic lȳt hafo
hēafodmāga nefne, Hygelāc, ðec.’
sentences.l: I have few of head-kinsmen, except, Higelac, you.’
sentences.i: I have few close kinsmen, Higelac, except you.’
sentences.n: ‘lȳt hafo’ is ‘I have little (few)’, ‘hafo’ being a first-person present of ‘habban’ with an older ending than ‘hæbbe’. ‘hēafodmāga’ is a genitive plural, ‘of head-kinsmen’, that is close or chief relatives (‘hēafod’ ‘head’ + ‘māg’ ‘kinsman’). ‘nefne’ is ‘except’, and ‘ðec’, the accusative of ‘ðū’ in its fuller form, ‘you’, is the one named in the exception. The closing quotation mark ends the whole report to Higelāc begun at 2000.

sentences.t:
Hēt ðā in beran eafor hēafodsegn,
heaðostēapne helm, hāre byrnan,
gūðsweord geatolīc, gyd æfter wræc:
sentences.l: Bade then in to bear the boar, the head-standard, the battle-high helmet, the grey byrnie, the splendid war-sword; afterwards he uttered a speech:
sentences.i: Then he bade them bear in the boar, the head-standard, the helmet towering in battle, the grey byrnie, the splendid war-sword, and afterwards he made a speech:
sentences.n: ‘Hēt’ is the past of ‘hātan’, ‘command’, and ‘in beran’ is ‘to bear in’; the person who commands, Beowulf, is not named, since he is the speaker who has just stopped. The things carried in are all accusatives: ‘eafor hēafodsegn’, ‘heaðostēapne helm’ (‘stēap’, ‘steep, lofty’, so a helmet high in battle), ‘hāre byrnan’ (‘hār’ ‘grey’, of the colour of mail), and ‘gūðsweord geatolīc’ (‘geatolīc’ ‘splendid, adorned’). Most editors print ‘eafor’ and ‘hēafodsegn’ as one word, ‘eaforhēafodsegn’ (apparatus), so ‘boar head-standard’, the crest of a helmet with a boar on it, and the pair would then be one thing; Klaeber prints two words, and I give both. ‘eafor’ is ‘boar’ and a boar figure is on helmets elsewhere in the poem. ‘gyd æfter wræc’ is ‘uttered a speech afterwards’: ‘gyd’ is a ‘formal song or speech’, ‘wræc’ the past of ‘wrecan’, here ‘utter’, with ‘æfter’ an adverb. The colon opens Beowulf’s words that follow.

sentences.t:
‘Mē ðis hildesceorp Hrōðgār sealde,
snotra fengel;
sentences.l: ‘To me Hrothgar gave this battle-garment, the wise prince;
sentences.i: ‘Hrothgar, the wise prince, gave me this armour;
sentences.n: The word order is object first, ‘Mē ðis hildesceorp Hrōðgār sealde’, ‘to me this war-gear Hrothgar gave’. ‘hildesceorp’ is ‘battle-garment’ (‘hilde’ ‘battle’ + ‘sceorp’ ‘clothing, equipment’), probably the ‘hāre byrnan’ of 2153, though ‘ðis’ may cover all the gear brought in. ‘snotra fengel’ is ‘wise prince’, in apposition to Hrothgar; ‘fengel’ is ‘prince, ruler’ and ‘snotra’ the weak nominative ‘wise’. Beowulf’s ‘Mē … sealde’ opens the speech; the quotation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
sume worde hēt,
þæt ic his ǣrest ðē ēst gesægde;
sentences.l: with a certain word he bade that I his favour first to you declare;
sentences.i: he charged me, in so many words, to tell you first of his goodwill;
sentences.n: ‘sume worde’ is ‘with a certain word’, an instrumental/dative of means and perhaps ‘expressly’; that this is the sense is a guess from the context. ‘hēt’ governs a clause with ‘þæt’, ‘ic … gesægde’, ‘that I should say’, from ‘gesecgan’; ‘gesægde’ has the same form in the indicative and the subjunctive, and the clause after ‘hēt’ asks for the subjunctive. The thing to be told is ‘ēst’, ‘favour, goodwill’ (accusative), with ‘his’, ‘Hrothgar’s’, and ‘ǣrest’ an adverb, ‘first’. Klaeber prints ‘ǣrest’ and ‘ēst’; Conybeare and Thorkelin would read ‘ǣrend’, ‘errand’, so ‘tell his errand first’, and Grein (queried) and Rieger ‘ǣrist’ (apparatus). I follow Klaeber: the favour of the gift is the first thing to be told.

sentences.t:
cwæð þæt hyt hæfde Hiorogār cyning,
lēod Scyldunga lange hwīle;
sentences.l: he said that Heorogar the king had it, the prince of the Scyldings, for a long while;
sentences.i: he said that King Heorogar, prince of the Scyldings, had owned it for a long time;
sentences.n: ‘cwæð’ is ‘said’ and ‘hyt’ ‘it’, the war-gear. ‘Hiorogār’ is Hrothgar’s elder brother, called ‘Heregār’ at 467, whom Hrothgar succeeded. ‘lēod Scyldunga’ is ‘man, prince of the Scyldings’ (‘lēod’ here a masculine ‘prince’, not the neuter ‘lēod’ ‘people’), and ‘lange hwīle’ is an accusative of duration, ‘for a long while’. The talk is of how long Heorogar had owned the armour before it passed to Hrothgar.

sentences.t:
nō ðȳ ǣr suna sīnum syllan wolde,
hwatum Heorowearde, þēah hē him hold wǣre,
brēostgewǣdu.
sentences.l: none the sooner would he give it to his son, to the bold Heoroweard, though he were loyal to him, the breast-garments.
sentences.i: yet he would not for all that give the breast-armour to his own son, bold Heoroweard, loyal though that son was to him.
sentences.n: ‘nō ðȳ ǣr’ is ‘none the sooner’ (‘ðȳ’ is an instrumental, ‘by that’, with ‘ǣr’ ‘earlier’), which here means that Heorogar did not hand the armour on even when you might have expected him to. ‘suna sīnum … hwatum Heorowearde’ are datives, ‘to his son, to the bold Heoroweard’ (‘hwat’ ‘bold’), Heorogar’s son. ‘þēah hē him hold wǣre’ is ‘though he were loyal to him’, with a subjunctive for what is conceded. ‘brēostgewǣdu’, ‘breast-garments’, is delayed to the end of the sentence and is the object of ‘syllan’, ‘give’, in the plural though the thing is one corselet. The stop after it is Klaeber’s, in mid-line.

sentences.t: Brūc ealles well!’
sentences.l: Enjoy all of it well!’
sentences.i: Make good use of it all!’
sentences.n: ‘Brūc’ is a singular imperative of ‘brūcan’, ‘enjoy, use’, which takes the genitive, so ‘ealles’ is ‘of all’ (‘all of it’); ‘well’ is ‘well’. The words are addressed to Higelāc, whether they are Beowulf’s own or Hrothgar’s parting charge that he repeats (the text does not mark which). The quotation mark closes the speech to the king; the next sentence is the poet’s again.

sentences.l: I heard that four horses, swiftly, alike, kept the track after the trappings, apple-fallow;
sentences.i: I have heard that four horses, all alike and apple-coloured, followed swiftly after the trappings;
sentences.n: ‘Hȳrde ic þæt’ is ‘I heard that’, the poet’s formula for passing on what is told; it is the one used at 62. ‘þām frætwum’ is a dative, ‘after the trappings’, and ‘lāst weardode’ is ‘kept the track’, so ‘followed’; the verb is singular where four horses is plural, and Kemble and others would print ‘weardodon’ (apparatus). ‘lungre’ is ‘swiftly’ (Clark Hall: ‘quickly, promptly’), ‘gelīce’ ‘alike, equally’ (both adverbs, ‘lungre’ going with the verb), and ‘æppelfealuwe’ ‘apple-fallow’, a nominative plural in apposition to the horses; ‘fealu’ is a yellowish or reddish brown, so ‘apple-coloured’ in the idiomatic version, and the exact shade is a guess. The horses are an accompaniment of the armour: Beowulf is giving Higelāc all four.

sentences.t:
hē him ēst getēah
mēara ond māðma. —
sentences.l: he granted him favour, of horses and of treasures. —
sentences.i: he showed him favour with horses and with treasures. —
sentences.n: ‘hē’ is now Beowulf, as ‘him’ is Higelāc. ‘getēah’ is the past of ‘getēon’, ‘bestow, grant’ (with ‘ēst’, ‘show favour’, as in the idiomatic version), and ‘ēst’ is its object, ‘favour’, with the genitives ‘mēara ond māðma’, ‘of horses and of treasures’, saying what the favour consisted of. The dash is Klaeber’s sign of a pause before the poet comments.

sentences.t:
Swā sceal mǣg dôn,
nealles inwitnet ōðrum bregdon
dyrnum cræfte, dēað rēn(ian)
hondgesteallan.
sentences.l: So shall a kinsman do, not at all weave a malice-net for another by secret craft, contrive death for his hand-companion.
sentences.i: So ought a kinsman to behave: he must never weave a net of malice against another by secret cunning, nor plan the death of his comrade-in-arms.
sentences.n: ‘Swā sceal mǣg dôn’ is ‘so shall a kinsman do’, as in the maxim at 1172 and 1534 (‘swā sceal man dôn’), and as in the prologue’s ‘Swā sceal (geong g)uma gōde gewyrcean’ (20); the circumflex of ‘dôn’ is Klaeber’s sign for a contracted vowel. ‘nealles’, ‘not at all’, brings in the negative commands, ‘inwitnet … bregdon’ and ‘dēað rēn(ian)’. ‘bregdon’ has an ending ‘-on’ where an infinitive would be ‘-an’; I take it as an infinitive with ‘sceal’, in line with ‘dôn’, but a plural subjunctive is also possible and this is a guess. ‘inwitnet’ is ‘malice-net’: ‘inwit’ is ‘evil, treachery’, and the picture is a net spread for a man, so a plot; ‘bregdan’ is ‘weave, draw’. ‘dyrnum cræfte’ is ‘by secret craft’, a dative of means. Kemble restored ‘rēn(ian)’, ‘contrive, arrange’; the manuscript’s edge is lost. ‘hondgesteallan’ is ‘hand-companion’ (‘gesteall’ ‘companion’), a comrade at arms, in the dative with ‘dēað’. The thought is the poet’s own rule for how kin behave, and it prepares for the story of Higelāc and Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Hygelāce wæs
nīða heardum nefa swȳðe hold,
ond gehwæðer ōðrum hrōþra gemyndig. —
sentences.l: To Higelac, hard in hostilities, the nephew was very loyal, and each to the other mindful of joys. —
sentences.i: Beowulf was very loyal to Higelac, hard in battle as he was, and each was mindful of the other’s good. —
sentences.n: ‘Hygelāce’ is a dative of relation, ‘to Higelāc’, with ‘heardum’ a strong dative singular agreeing with it, ‘hard’; ‘nīða’ is a genitive plural, ‘in hostilities’ or ‘in strife’. ‘nefa’ is the subject, ‘the nephew’ (Beowulf), with ‘swȳðe hold’, ‘very loyal’, after ‘wæs’. ‘gehwæðer’ is ‘each of the two’, ‘ōðrum’ ‘to the other’, and ‘hrōþra gemyndig’, ‘mindful of’ plus a genitive plural of ‘hrōþor’, ‘benefit, comfort, joy’; I take ‘hrōþor’ in that sense, which is rare, so the exact word is a guess. The dash is Klaeber’s and ends the comment on kin.

sentences.t:
Hȳrde ic þæt hē ðone healsbēah Hygde gesealde,
wrǣtlicne wundụrmāððum, ðone þe him Wealhðēo geaf,
ðēod(nes) dohtor, þrīo wicg somod
swancor ond sadolbeorht;
sentences.l: I heard that he gave the neck-ring to Hygd, the wondrous wonder-treasure, which Wealhtheow gave him, the prince’s daughter, three horses together, supple and saddle-bright;
sentences.i: I have heard that he gave Hygd the neck-ring, that marvellous treasure which Wealhtheow, a prince’s daughter, had given him, together with three horses, supple and bright with saddles;
sentences.n: ‘Hȳrde ic þæt hē’ is the poet’s formula again, and ‘hē’ is Beowulf. ‘healsbēah’ is ‘neck-ring’ (‘heals’ ‘neck’ + ‘bēah’ ‘ring’), a collar of gold and a mark of rank; ‘Hygde’ is the dative of Hygd, Higelāc’s queen. ‘wrǣtlicne wundụrmāððum’ is ‘wondrous wonder-treasure’, both words accusative singular masculine in apposition to ‘healsbēah’ (the dot under the ‘u’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; it changes nothing in the sense). ‘ðone þe him Wealhðēo geaf’ is a relative clause, ‘which Wealhtheow gave him’: she gave Beowulf this ring in Heorot, told at 1192–1195, where the gifts brought to him include ‘healsbēaga mǣst’, ‘the greatest of neck-rings’, and at 1202 the poet goes on to say that Higelāc wore that ring on his last raid (1202–1214); how it came back to Beowulf is not told, so the poem here gives a second history of it. ‘ðēod(nes) dohtor’ is ‘the prince’s daughter’, an addition to ‘Wealhðēo’: Kemble restored the lost ending ‘(nes)’, the manuscript having only ‘ðēod’. ‘þrīo wicg’ is ‘three horses’, also accusative, given along with the ring, and ‘somod’ ‘together’. ‘swancor’ is ‘lithe, supple’ and ‘sadolbeorht’ ‘saddle-bright’, ‘bright with a saddle’; the phrase probably means saddled with bright trappings and is a guess.

sentences.t:
hyre syððan wæs
æfter bēahðege br[ē]ost geweorðod.
sentences.l: to her afterwards, after the ring-taking, the breast was adorned.
sentences.i: and after receiving the ring her breast was adorned.
sentences.n: ‘hyre’ is a dative, ‘to her’, serving as a possessive with ‘brēost’, ‘breast’. ‘æfter bēahðege’ is ‘after the ring-taking’ (‘ðege’ is ‘receiving’, from ‘þicgan’, ‘receive’), ‘geweorðod’ ‘adorned, honoured’, a past participle. Thorkelin supplied the ‘ē’ in ‘br[ē]ost’; the manuscript has ‘brost’. So the ring Beowulf had from Wealhtheow ends as an ornament of Hygd.

sentences.l: So was bold the son of Ecgtheow, the man known in wars, in good deeds, he lived after glory;
sentences.i: So the son of Ecgtheow acted boldly, a man known in battles; by good deeds he lived for renown;
sentences.n: ‘bealdode’ is the past of ‘bealdian’, ‘be bold, act boldly’. ‘guma gūðum cūð’ is ‘a man known in wars’ (‘cūð’ ‘known’ with a dative plural), and ‘gōdum dǣdum’ ‘by good deeds’, a dative of means. ‘drēah’ is the past of ‘drēogan’, ‘do, perform, live’, with ‘æfter dōme’, ‘after glory’, which I take as ‘living for glory’. ‘dōm’ is both ‘judgement’ (2147) and ‘glory, repute’, here the second. ‘bearn Ecgðēowes’ is the poem’s usual name for Beowulf.

sentences.t:
nealles druncne slōg
heorðgenēatas;
sentences.l: not at all did he slay drunken hearth-companions;
sentences.i: he never struck down his hearth-companions in their drink;
sentences.n: ‘druncne’ is an accusative plural masculine, so it goes with ‘heorðgenēatas’ and not with the subject: the hearth-companions are drunk, not Beowulf. The line says he did not strike down hearth-companions who were drunk. ‘heorðgenēatas’ is ‘hearth-companions’ (‘heorð’ ‘hearth’ + ‘genēat’ ‘companion’), the retinue that lives at the lord’s fire. The poem has already given the opposite in Heremod, who in anger cut down his table-companions and shoulder-companions (1713–1714); I take the remark to be set against that, but the text does not say so.

sentences.t:
næs him hrēoh sefa,
ac hē mancynnes mǣste cræfte
ginfæstan gife, þē him God sealde,
hēold hildedēor.
sentences.l: was not to him a fierce mind, but he, with the greatest strength of mankind, held the ample gift which God gave him, battle-brave.
sentences.i: His heart was not savage, but he, the strongest of mankind, kept the great gift that God had given him, a man brave in battle.
sentences.n: ‘næs him hrēoh sefa’ is ‘was not to him a fierce mind’; ‘hrēoh’ is ‘rough, fierce’. ‘mancynnes mǣste cræfte’ I take as ‘with the greatest strength of mankind’: ‘mancynnes’ is a genitive, ‘of mankind’, and ‘mǣste’ is the superlative in the instrumental, agreeing with ‘cræfte’ (it cannot be a nominative masculine, which would be ‘mǣsta’); ‘cræft’ is strength in the old sense, power. The phrase belongs to ‘hē’, so the sense is that he was the strongest of men; the loose grammar makes this my reading. ‘ginfæstan gife’ is ‘the ample gift’ (‘ginfæst’ ‘richly endowed, ample’, ‘gife’ a feminine accusative), the object of ‘hēold’, with ‘þē him God sealde’ a relative clause, ‘which God gave him’. ‘hildedēor’ is ‘battle-brave’, nominative in apposition to ‘hē’. I take the ‘gift’ to be his great strength, and that it comes from God is the poet’s Christian note.

sentences.t:
Hēan wæs lange,
swā hyne Gēata bearn gōdne ne tealdon,
nē hyne on medobence micles wyrðne
drihten Wedera gedōn wolde;
sentences.l: Despised he was long, as the sons of the Geats did not reckon him good, nor would the lord of the Weders make him of much worth on the mead-bench;
sentences.i: He was held in low esteem for a long time, for the Geats did not think him good, nor would the lord of the Weders rank him as worth much on the mead-bench;
sentences.n: ‘Hēan’ is ‘lowly, despised’, a predicate adjective, and ‘lange’ ‘a long time’. ‘swā’ here is ‘as, inasmuch as’ (a result, ‘so that’, is also possible); ‘gōdne ne tealdon’ is ‘did not reckon (him) good’, from ‘tellan’, and ‘nē … gedōn wolde’ ‘nor would (he) make’, with ‘micles wyrðne’, ‘worth of much’ (genitive ‘micles’ after ‘wyrðne’), so ‘rate him highly’. ‘medobenc’ is the bench in the hall where the drink was served, so the line speaks of his standing at table. ‘Wedera’ is Klaeber’s italic reading: the manuscript has ‘wereda’, a genitive plural of ‘weorod’, ‘of hosts’, and Holthausen, Sedgefield and Chambers (with an earlier suggestion in the apparatus) read ‘Wedera’; so ‘drihten Wedera’ is ‘lord of the Weders’, Higelāc, the name Weders being another for the Geats. The manuscript reading would give ‘lord of hosts’, which makes sense but fits less well here. This is the old report of his slow youth, told by the poet and not by Beowulf.

sentences.t:
swȳðe (wēn)don, þæt hē slēac wǣre,
æðeling unfrom.
sentences.l: greatly they supposed that he was slack, an atheling unvaliant.
sentences.i: They firmly believed that he was slack, a prince without vigour.
sentences.n: ‘swȳðe’ is ‘greatly, strongly’, and ‘wēndon’ ‘thought, supposed’, plural past; Grein restored the lost letters in ‘(wēn)don’. ‘þæt hē slēac wǣre’ takes a subjunctive after a verb of thinking, ‘that he was slack’ (‘slēac’ ‘slack, sluggish’). ‘æðeling unfrom’ is ‘a prince unvaliant’, ‘unfrom’ being ‘not bold, not vigorous’ (‘from’ ‘strong, bold’); the exact sense of ‘unfrom’ is a guess. ‘æðeling’ is a man of noble birth or a prince; Beowulf is Higelāc’s nephew.

sentences.t:
Edwenden cwōm
tīrēadịgum menn torna gehwylces. —
sentences.l: A reversal came to the glory-blessed man of each of the sorrows. —
sentences.i: A turn of fortune came to the glorious man, an end to every one of his sorrows. —
sentences.n: ‘Edwenden’ is ‘reversal, turn’ (‘ed-’ ‘again, back’ + ‘wenden’ ‘turning’), a noun and the subject of ‘cwōm’, ‘came’. ‘tīrēadịgum menn’ is a dative, ‘to the man blessed with glory’ (‘tīr’ ‘glory’ + ‘ēadig’ ‘blessed, prosperous’; the dot is Klaeber’s metrical sign), and ‘torna gehwylces’ a genitive, ‘of each of the sorrows’ (‘torn’ ‘grief, anger, humiliation’). The turn begins with Higelāc’s gifts in the next lines.

sentences.l: Bade then the shelter of earls bring in, the battle-famed king, Hrethel’s heirloom, adorned with gold;
sentences.i: Then the protector of earls, the battle-famous king, ordered Hrethel’s heirloom to be brought in, adorned with gold;
sentences.n: ‘Hēt’ is ‘bade’ and ‘in gefetian’ ‘to fetch in’; the subject is ‘eorla hlēo’, ‘shelter of earls’ (as of Hrothgar at 2142), and ‘heaðorōf cyning’, ‘battle-famous king’, both Higelāc. The object is ‘Hrēðles lāfe’, ‘Hrethel’s heirloom’ (‘lāf’ ‘what is left, legacy’), with ‘golde gegyrede’, ‘adorned with gold’ (a past participle, accusative feminine). Hrethel was Higelāc’s father and Beowulf’s grandfather. The next line shows that the heirloom is a sword.

sentences.t:
næs mid Gēatum ðā
sincmāðþụm sēlra on sweordes hād;
sentences.l: there was not then among the Geats a better one among treasures in the form of a sword;
sentences.i: there was then among the Geats no finer treasure in the shape of a sword;
sentences.n: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’; ‘sēlra’ is a comparative, ‘better’, with the dative ‘sincmāðþụm’, ‘among treasures’ (or, as a dative of comparison, ‘better than treasures’) (‘sinc’ ‘treasure’ + ‘māððum’ ‘precious thing’; the dot is Klaeber’s metrical sign). ‘on sweordes hād’ is ‘in the form of a sword’, ‘hād’ ‘condition, rank, form’. ‘Mid Gēatum’ is ‘among the Geats’. The sentence says no sword among the Geats was a greater treasure.

sentences.t:
þæt hē on Bīowulfes bearm ālegde,
ond him gesealde seofan þūsendo,
bold ond bregostōl.
sentences.l: which he laid in Beowulf’s lap, and gave him seven thousand, a hall and a princely seat.
sentences.i: He laid it in Beowulf’s lap and gave him seven thousand, a hall and a throne.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is a neuter pronoun, ‘that’ or ‘which’ (the sword), the object of ‘ālegde’, ‘laid’, with ‘on Bīowulfes bearm’, ‘into Beowulf’s lap’ (‘bearm’ ‘lap, bosom’, an accusative of motion). ‘seofan þūsendo’ is ‘seven thousand’, with no noun; the next lines speak of land, and ‘hides’ of land is the usual guess, so that is a guess. ‘bold ond bregostōl’ is ‘a hall and a princely seat’ (‘brego’ ‘prince, lord’ + ‘stōl’ ‘seat’), the throne of a lord, standing for rank. The two nouns are accusatives in apposition to the gift.

sentences.t:
Him wæs bām samod
on ðām lēodscipe lond gecynde,
eard ēðelriht, ōðrum swīðor
sīde rīce þām ðǣr sēlra wæs.
sentences.l: To both of them together in that people-realm land was inborn, homestead, native right, to the one more, wide rule, to him who there was better.
sentences.i: Both of them held land by birth in that nation, a homestead and a hereditary right, though the wider rule belonged to the one who was the higher there.
sentences.n: ‘Him … bām’ is a dative, ‘to both of them’, Higelāc and Beowulf; ‘lond gecynde’ is ‘land inborn’ (‘gecynde’ ‘natural, hereditary’), and ‘eard ēðelriht’ two more nouns beside it, ‘homestead, native right’. ‘lēodscipe’ is ‘nation, people-realm’. The last two lines are hard: ‘ōðrum swīðor’ is ‘to the one more’ (literally ‘to the other’, the second member of the pair), and ‘sīde rīce’, ‘wide rule’, with ‘þām ðǣr sēlra wæs’, ‘to him who there was better (higher)’. I read it as ‘both had land by birthright, but the larger kingdom was the king’s’, Higelāc being the one ‘sēlra’; the exact reading of ‘ōðrum swīðor’ is a guess. What is clear is that the gift gives Beowulf a place in the kingdom, not just a sword.

sentences.t:
Eft þæt geīode ufaran dōgrum
hildehlæmmum, syððan Hygelāc læg,
ond Hear[dr]ēde hildemēceas
under bordhrēoðan tō bonan wurdon,
sentences.l: Again that came to pass in later days, in the battle-crashes, after Higelac lay, and to Heardred battle-swords under the shield-cover became slayers,
sentences.i: Later, in days of crashing battle, it came about that after Higelac had fallen and swords of war had become Heardred’s slayers beneath his shield-cover,
sentences.n: ‘Eft’ is ‘afterwards’, ‘geīode’ the past of ‘gegān’, ‘happened’, ‘þæt’ ‘that’ (the following matter), and ‘ufaran dōgrum’ ‘in later days’, a dative plural. ‘hildehlæmmum’ is a dative of manner, ‘in battle-crashes’ (‘hlem’ ‘crash, clash’). ‘syððan Hygelāc læg’ is ‘after Higelāc lay’, that is, lay dead. ‘Hear[dr]ēde’ is a dative: the manuscript has ‘hearede’, and Grundtvig supplied ‘dr’, giving Heardrēd, Higelāc’s son. ‘hildemēceas’ is ‘battle-swords’, nominative plural, ‘under bordhrēoðan’ ‘under the shield-cover’, and ‘tō bonan wurdon’ ‘became slayers (to him)’, an idiom with the dative of the one killed. The sentence runs on to 2206 and is only finished at 2207.

sentences.t:
ðā hyne gesōhtan on sigeþēode
hearde hildfrecan, Heaðo-Scilfingas,
nīða genǣgdan nefan Hererīces —:
sentences.l: when the hard battle-bold ones, the War-Scylfings, sought him out among the victory-people, assailed the nephew of Hereric in hostilities —:
sentences.i: when the hard fighters, the War-Scylfings, sought him out among the victorious people and attacked Hereric’s nephew in battle —:
sentences.n: ‘ðā’ is the conjunction ‘when’, and ‘hyne’ is ‘him’, Heardrēd. ‘gesōhtan’ is ‘sought out’, ‘hearde hildfrecan’ ‘hard battle-bold ones’, in apposition with ‘Heaðo-Scilfingas’, the War-Scylfings, the Swedes. Klaeber’s italic ‘d’ in ‘hildfrecan’ marks his change from the manuscript’s ‘hilde’; the sense is little altered, since ‘hilde frecan’ in two words would also be ‘bold in battle’. ‘on sigeþēode’ is ‘among the victory-people’, probably the Geats, a guess. ‘nīða genǣgdan’ is ‘assailed with hostilities’, ‘genǣgdan’ from ‘genǣgan’, ‘attack’ (the genitive plural ‘nīða’ is used as a means; a guess). ‘nefan Hererīces’ is ‘the nephew of Hereric’, an accusative, Heardrēd. Who Hereric was is not said; as the uncle, he is perhaps Hygd’s brother, a guess. The dash and colon mark a pause before the main clause that follows.

sentences.t:
syððan Bēowulfe brāde rīce
on hand gehwearf;
sentences.l: after to Beowulf the broad realm came into his hand;
sentences.i: after the broad kingdom passed into Beowulf’s hand;
sentences.n: ‘syððan’ here again means ‘after’; ‘Bēowulfe’ is a dative, ‘to Beowulf’, and ‘brāde rīce’ ‘the broad kingdom’ is the subject of ‘gehwearf’, the past of ‘gehweorfan’, ‘turn, pass’; ‘on hand’ is ‘into hand’, in his keeping. This is the main statement of the long sentence that began at 2200: the kingdom passed to him after the falls of Higelāc and Heardrēd. The page of the manuscript, folio 179, is the worst of the whole, freshened up by a later hand and not always correctly, so the readings from here are often disputed; the notes will say so where it matters.

sentences.t:
hē gehēold tela
fīftig wintra — wæs ðā frōd cyning,
eald ēþelweard —,
sentences.l: he held it well fifty winters — he was then a wise king, an old guardian of the homeland —,
sentences.i: he ruled it well for fifty winters — he was by then a wise king, an old guardian of his homeland —,
sentences.n: ‘hē gehēold tela’ is ‘he held (ruled) well’, ‘fīftig wintra’ an accusative of duration, ‘fifty of winters’. The manuscript has ‘wintru’ in a later hand (apparatus), no change of sense. The two phrases between the dashes are asides: ‘wæs ðā frōd cyning’, ‘was then a wise king’ (‘frōd’ ‘wise by age, old’), and ‘eald ēþelweard’, ‘an old homeland-guardian’ (‘ēþel’ ‘homeland’ + ‘weard’ ‘guardian’), as at 1702 (‘eald ēþelweard’, rendered ‘old guardian of the homeland’ in fitt-24). Thorkelin, Rieger and Sedgefield read ‘þæt for ðā’ for ‘wæs ðā’ (apparatus), which would change the clause.

sentences.t:
oð ðæt ān ongan
deorcum nihtum draca rīcs[i]an,
sentences.l: until one began in dark nights to rule, a dragon,
sentences.i: until a dragon began to hold sway in the dark nights,
sentences.n: ‘oð ðæt’ is ‘until’, ‘ān’ ‘one, a certain one’, which the next word names, ‘draca’, a dragon, in apposition. ‘ongan’ is ‘began’, followed by the infinitive ‘rīcs[i]an’, ‘hold sway, rule’; the manuscript has ‘ricsan’, and Kemble supplied the ‘i’. ‘deorcum nihtum’ is ‘in dark nights’, a dative of time. The apparatus says a later hand has ‘ón’ in this half-line (2210b), probably for ‘ān’, the freshened page being unreliable. The dragon’s rule is placed in the dark nights.

sentences.t:
sē ðe on hēa(ụm) h(ǣþ)e hord beweotode,
stānbeorh stēapne;
sentences.l: who on the high heath guarded a hoard, a steep stone-barrow;
sentences.i: who watched over a hoard on the high heath, a steep barrow of stone;
sentences.n: ‘sē ðe’ is ‘he who’, the dragon, with ‘beweotode’, ‘kept watch over’. ‘hord’ is ‘hoard’, and ‘stānbeorh stēapne’ ‘a steep stone-barrow’ (‘stān’ ‘stone’ + ‘beorh’ ‘mound, barrow’), a second accusative. The place is the trouble: in the manuscript the letters between ‘hea’ and ‘hord’ are very indistinct, and Zupitza read ‘heaðo hlæwe’, ‘battle-mound’, but Klaeber finds that ‘ðo’ is too short and ‘hlæwe’ too long for the space; Chambers seems to see ‘um’ and then ‘hæþe’ (Sievers) or ‘hope’ (himself). I give Sedgefield’s reading, which Klaeber prints with parentheses and a dot: ‘hēa(ụm) h(ǣþ)e’, ‘on the high heath’ (‘hēaum’ a strong dative singular, masculine or neuter, ‘hǣþe’ the dative of ‘hǣþ’, ‘heath’). It is a restoration, and the sense is disputed. ‘hope’ would be a secluded or enclosed place (Bosworth–Toller, ‘hop’).

sentences.t:
stīg under læg
eldum uncūð.
sentences.l: a path lay under it, unknown to men.
sentences.i: a path lay beneath it that was unknown to men.
sentences.n: ‘stīg’ is ‘path’, the subject, ‘under læg’ ‘lay beneath’, and ‘eldum uncūð’ ‘unknown to men’ (‘eldum’ a dative plural of ‘ylde’, ‘ielde’, which is a plural noun meaning ‘men’). The path leads in below the mound and is the thing that someone is soon going to find. ‘under’ I take as ‘beneath the mound’, a guess from what follows.

sentences.t:
Þǣr on innan gīong
nið[ð]a nāthwylc, (forþ nē)h gefe(al)g
hǣðnum horde,
sentences.l: There within went some one or other of men, forth near pressed on to the heathen hoard,
sentences.i: Into it there went some man or other, and he pressed close up to the heathen hoard,
sentences.n: ‘Þǣr on innan gīong’ is ‘there within went’, ‘gīong’ the past of ‘gangan’. ‘nið[ð]a nāthwylc’ is ‘some one or other of men’: ‘nāthwylc’ is ‘ne wāt hwylc’, ‘I do not know which’, and ‘nið[ð]a’ a genitive plural of ‘niðð’, ‘man, mortal’; Kluge supplied the second ‘ð’, the manuscript presumably having ‘niða’ (the apparatus does not say). The manuscript is damaged in the next words: the leaf has ‘h gefe : (:) g’ (apparatus) and Klaeber restores ‘(forþ nē)h gefe(al)g’, ‘forth, near, pressed’, from ‘gefeolan’, which I take to mean ‘penetrate, come to’. ‘hǣðnum horde’ is a dative, ‘to the heathen hoard’, ‘hǣðen’ ‘heathen’, the hoard of pagans. For the lost words Sedgefield reads ‘sē (þe) n(ē)h geþ(ra)ng’, and Bugge ‘nēode tō gefēng’, ‘by need laid hold’; Klaeber’s restoration is only one of several. The thief is unnamed, and ‘nāthwylc’ is the poet’s way of saying he does not tell us who.

sentences.t:
hond (wǣge nam),
(sīd,) since fāh;
sentences.l: with his hand took a large cup, adorned with treasure;
sentences.i: he took in his hand a great cup, bright with treasure;
sentences.n: Almost all of this is restored: ‘(wǣge nam)’, ‘took a cup’, and ‘(sīd,)’, ‘large’, are Klaeber’s additions: for ‘(wǣge nam)’ he follows Trautmann, who read ‘hond (wǣge nam), (sigle) since fāch’ (apparatus), but ‘(sīd,)’ stands in place of Trautmann’s ‘(sigle)’. ‘hond’ I take as a dative of means, ‘with the hand’. ‘wǣge’ is ‘cup, flagon’, ‘sīd’ ‘large, wide’, and ‘since fāh’ ‘adorned with treasure’: ‘fāh’ is ‘stained, variegated, bright’ and the dative ‘since’ says with what. The manuscript originally had ‘fac’ with an ‘h’ written over the ‘c’ (apparatus). Sedgefield reads ‘since fāhne’ (accusative). Bugge’s restoration for this lost stretch gives a different sentence, ‘hond ætgenam seleful since fāh’, ‘took a hall-cup bright with treasure’, much like this one in sense. The sense that a cup is the thing taken is therefore fairly safe; the words themselves are guesses.

sentences.l: nor did he afterwards conceal that, though sleeping he was ensnared by the thief’s craft;
sentences.i: nor did the dragon afterwards hide it, though he was tricked in his sleep by the thief’s cunning;
sentences.n: ‘nē hē þæt syððan (bemāð)’ is ‘nor he that afterwards (concealed)’: ‘bemāð’ is the past of ‘bemīðan’, ‘hide, conceal’, restored in Anglia xxviii; the subject ‘hē’ is then the dragon, and ‘þæt’ is what has just happened to him, which the next lines say the people found out (that he was enraged). Bugge’s restoration gives ‘āgeaf’, ‘gave back’, and Sedgefield ‘(wræc)’ in place of ‘(bemāð)’, either of which would change the sense; I follow Klaeber. The next clause is damaged too: ‘þ(ēah) ð(e hē)’, ‘though he’, is from the manuscript as Zupitza read it, and ‘besyre(d wur)de’, ‘was ensnared’, from Kluge; ‘besyrwan’ is ‘ensnare, deceive’. ‘slǣpende’ is ‘sleeping’, ‘þēofes cræfte’ ‘by the thief’s craft’, a dative of means. On this reading the dragon was tricked while asleep.

sentences.t:
þæt sīe ðīod (onfand),
b(ig)folc beorna, þæt hē gebolge(n) wæs.
sentences.l: that the people discovered, the neighbour-folk of men, that he was enraged.
sentences.i: and the people found it out, the neighbouring folk of men, that he was in a rage.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is first the pronoun, ‘that’, the object of ‘(onfand)’, ‘discovered’ (Grein’s restoration; ‘onfindan’), and then the conjunction of ‘þæt hē gebolge(n) wæs’, ‘that he was enraged’, with Grein’s ‘n’ at the lost edge. ‘sīe’ is the spelling Klaeber prints (AB have ‘sie’); I take it as the feminine ‘the’ (‘sēo’, ‘sīo’) with ‘ðīod’, a variant spelling of ‘ðēod’, ‘people’, the subject of ‘(onfand)’. Kluge would print ‘sīo’, which may be the original reading before the page was freshened up (apparatus). ‘b(ig)folc beorna’ is ‘neighbour-folk of men’: the first part of the word is lost and the manuscript has apparently ‘bu’ or ‘by’; Bugge reads ‘(bȳ)folc’, Trautmann, Sedgefield and Chambers ‘(bū)folc’, ‘dwelling-folk’, Kluge and Holthausen ‘(burh)folc’, ‘city-folk’, which is too long, and Klaeber ‘(big)folc’, which I take to be ‘folk living by’, a guess. Thorkelin’s transcript has ‘….folcbiorn’ (apparatus). ‘beorna’ is a genitive plural, ‘of men’. The sentence ends here, and 2221 begins a new one.
